title: Presses and papers
hook: Gurmukhi newspapers and presses spread the reform

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Karaj, and the lavan recognized in law. Today, how word of causes like that one traveled from town to town.

Ink on fingers. In a back room in Lahore, a typesetter picks small metal letters out of a wooden case, one by one, and lines them up in a frame. They're Gurmukhi letters, the same shapes a reader meets on a page of the Granth. A lever comes down, the press clanks, and a sheet lifts off with the ink still wet. Soon it will be folded, bundled, and carried to another town.
screen: `METAL LETTERS, SET BY HAND.` → `THE SHAPES OF THE GRANTH.` → `A SHEET, STILL WET.`

segments.voice: First, the script. Gurmukhi is the alphabet the Gurus used for their hymns; tradition credits Guru Angad with shaping it for Sikh use. To print in Gurmukhi was to print in the letters of the Granth, so a newspaper set in that type could double as a reading lesson for the scripture. Second, the papers. Reformers started newspapers in Punjabi. The Khalsa Akhbar came out of Lahore, linked to the scholar Giani Ditt Singh. In Amritsar, Bhai Vir Singh, the poet you met a few days ago, ran the Khalsa Samachar. They carried news, arguments about reform, explanations of Sikh history and practice, and appeals for schools and causes. Third, the tracts: small, cheap booklets on single subjects, a Guru's life, the meaning of a hymn, how to hold a ceremony. Vir Singh helped found a society to publish them. A tract could be bought for a coin, read in an evening, passed to a neighbor. Fourth, why print mattered. The Gurus had gathered their hymns into a book so the word could be kept and shared. Near the end of the Granth, Guru Arjan speaks of a dish holding truth, contentment and reflection, and Sikh tradition hears that dish as the Granth itself. Print was another way of laying that dish out for everyone. A movement of a few learned men became a conversation in many households. Arguments still broke out, sometimes fierce ones, but they broke out among people who were reading.
screen: `THE LETTERS OF THE GRANTH.` · `PAPERS IN LAHORE AND AMRITSAR.` · `A TRACT FOR A COIN.` · `A WHOLE COMMUNITY READING.` · then, large: `PRINT SPREADS IT.`

segments.voice: Choose one Punjabi word you already know from this path, Waheguru, sangat, seva, langar or Khalsa, and picture it written in Gurmukhi, even if you don't know the letters: curved shapes hanging from a line at the top. Breathe in and hear the word; breathe out and let it rest.
Akhbar, newspaper, a word Punjabi shares with Persian and Urdu: the Gurmukhi papers, presses and tracts that carried the reform into households across the Punjab. Today's word.
Your line: print spreads it. Not only news, but a habit: Sikhs reading their own story in their own letters. Back soon, same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Sikh newspapers, magazines and publishers still print in Gurmukhi and English, and gurdwaras often keep free booklets on Sikh history and practice for visitors to take home.

chat.says: How did the Singh Sabha reform reach so many Sikh homes?
options: Through Punjabi papers and cheap tracts printed in Gurmukhi and passed hand to hand.
Mostly through English books written for British officials and scholars.
Only through speeches, since few Punjabi books were ever printed then.
chat.meaning: Papers like the Khalsa Akhbar and Khalsa Samachar, and tracts sold for a coin, carried the reform into many households.
